name: Augustan and Eighteenth-Century Period
description: English literature from the accession of the Hanoverians to the outbreak of the French Revolution, covering Augustan satire and neoclassical criticism, the periodical essay, the rise of the novel, the regenerated London stage, sentimental and graveyard verse, the Enlightenment in England and Scotland, evangelical revival, the bluestocking circle, and the first feminist and abolitionist polemics.
historical_context: The period opens with the Act of Settlement (1701) and the Hanoverian succession (1714), the Whig oligarchy, the Union with Scotland (1707), the South Sea bubble (1720), the Jacobite risings (1715, 1745), the Stationers' Copyright Act (1710), the rise of party journalism and daily print, the middle ranks' growing commercial prosperity, the Seven Years War, the loss and recovery of empire, the beginnings of the abolitionist campaign (Somerset's case, 1772), and the American and French Revolutions. The Regency crisis, Wilkes and the liberty of the press, and the growth of provincial and Scottish intellectual culture in Edinburgh and Glasgow reshape the literary map.
literary_characteristics: A literature of public argument: wit, ridicule, decorum and the 'rules' dominate the first half; the periodical essay, the character, the sermon and the pamphlet create a daily prose style. Verse moves from heroic couplet satire and the estate poem to the blank-verse meditation, the ode and the ballad. Prose fiction matures from Defoe's factual imposture through Richardson's epistolary analysis and Fielding's comic-epic to Sterne's experimental self-consciousness, the sentimental and gothic novel, and the Scottish historical tale. Criticism (Addison, Pope, Johnson, Kames, Blair, Reid, Adam Smith) becomes a self-conscious discipline; the novel, the theatre and the periodical are all debated in the same print public.
